thesis: Whether every detail of an organism's structure must be explained as useful (adaptive), i.e. as shaped by natural selection (Darwin first says every detail is of use to the organism or its ancestors, later admits structures that are neither beneficial nor injurious and that he over-attributed to natural selection).

early.text: Hence every detail of structure in every living creature (making some little allowance for the direct action of physical conditions) may be viewed, either as having been of special use to some ancestral form, or as being now of special use to the descendants of this form—either directly, or indirectly through the complex laws of growth.
early.work: On the Origin of Species (1st ed.), Chapter VI "Difficulties on Theory"
early.locator: Chapter VI, section on the utilitarian doctrine

announced.text: Nevertheless, I did not formerly consider sufficiently the existence of structures, which, as far as we can at present judge, are neither beneficial nor injurious; and this I believe to be one of the greatest oversights as yet detected in my work.
announced.work: The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex (2nd ed. text)
announced.locator: Part I, Chapter II (end), the paragraph after "I now admit, after reading the essay by Nageli"

unannounced.text: We can, in our ignorance of most of the lowest animals, only say that their bright tints result either from the chemical nature or the minute structure of their tissues, independently of any benefit thus derived. Hardly any colour is finer than that of arterial blood; but there is no reason to suppose that the colour of the blood is in itself any advantage; and though it adds to the beauty of the maiden’s cheek, no one will pretend that it has been acquired for this purpose.
unannounced.work: The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex (2nd ed. text)
unannounced.locator: CHAPTER IX., section on colours of the lowest animals (before "The Sub-kingdom of the Mollusca")

control.text: In a state of nature almost every plant produces seed, and amongst animals there are very few which do not annually pair. Hence we may confidently assert, that all plants and animals are tending to increase at a geometrical ratio, that all would most rapidly stock every station in which they could any how exist, and that the geometrical tendency to increase must be checked by destruction at some period of life.
control.work: On the Origin of Species (1st ed.), Chapter III "Struggle for Existence"
control.locator: Chapter III, early section (geometrical ratio of increase)

notes: Gutenberg #2300 is the 1874 second-edition text of the Descent (Darwin's preface to it is included but outside the span); the Nageli/Broca admission is a passage Darwin added to Origin's 5th ed. (1869) and the Descent's 1871 first ed.; I have not checked the 1871 printing itself, only the 1874 text used. The early passage sits in a paragraph that already concedes 'many structures are of no direct use' and hedges 'some little allowance'; the conflict with the later view is one of degree/emphasis, as Darwin himself frames it. Secondary page is Wikipedia (not SEP/IEP): it records Nageli's objection and that Darwin conceded the point.

thesis: Whether the Church of Rome is the Anglican's enemy and a corrupt, hostile body (Newman's Anglican view of Rome, which he later renounced on becoming a Catholic).

early.text: We must take and deal with things as they are, not as they pretend to be. If we are induced to believe the professions of Rome, and make advances towards her as if a sister or a mother Church, which in theory she is, we shall find too late that we are in the arms of a pitiless and unnatural relative, who will but triumph in the arts which have inveigled us within her reach.
early.work: Lectures on the Prophetical Office of the Church (Via Media vol. 1, 3rd ed. text), Lecture 3

announced.text: But now, as to the third point on which I stood in 1833, and which I have utterly renounced and trampled upon since,--my then view of the Church of Rome;--I will speak about it as exactly as I can. When I was young, as I have said already, and after I was grown up, I thought the Pope to be Antichrist. At Christmas 1824-5 I preached a sermon to that effect.
announced.work: Apologia pro Vita Sua (1890 ed.), Chapter II
announced.locator: Chapter II, "third point" (view of the Church of Rome)

control.text: Such is the feeling of minds unversed in the disappointments of the world, incredulous how much it has of promise, how little of substance; what intricacy and confusion beset the most certain truths; how much must be taken on trust, in order to be possessed; how little can be realized except by an effort of the will; how great a part of enjoyment lies in resignation.
control.work: Lectures on the Prophetical Office of the Church (Via Media vol. 1, 3rd ed. text), Lecture 14

notes: Early text is from newmanreader.org (not Gutenberg/IA): the 1877 Via Media reprint of the 1837 lectures. I saved only each lecture's body (stopped before the 1877 footnotes, which are by the later Catholic Newman) and kept the site's {page} and [Note n] markers, which the chosen passages avoid. I cross-checked the passage against the 1837 first-edition OCR on archive.org (p. 101): same words. The Cambridge Church History article says the offending language of p. 101 of the Lectures was later retracted (its note 49, citing Via Media 2:429-431). The announced passage says Newman 'utterly renounced' his 1833 view of Rome but does not itself describe the new view; note Newman insists in the Apologia that the 1843 retractation withdrew the saying, not necessarily the belief at the time. No unannounced passage; the Apologia is Newman's only later text collected here.

thesis: Whether a Socialist/Communist organisation of society would destroy individual freedom and so should be opposed (Mill's hostile first-edition treatment of Socialism, later cancelled and replaced by a more favourable one).

early.text: The perfection of social arrangements would be to secure to all persons complete independence and freedom of action, subject to no restriction but that of not doing injury to others: but the scheme which we are considering abrogates this freedom entirely, and places every action of every member of the community under command.
early.work: Principles of Political Economy, 1st ed. (1848), vol. 1, Book II ch. I section 3 "Communism"

announced.text: In the first edition the difficulties of Socialism were stated so strongly, that the tone was on the whole that of opposition to it. In the year or two which followed, much time was given to the study of the best Socialistic writers on the Continent, and to meditation and discussion on the whole range of topics involved in the controversy: and the result was that most of what had been written on the subject in the first edition was cancelled, and replaced by arguments and reflections which represent a more advanced opinion.

control.text: We may rather compare it to a highly elastic and extensible band, which is hardly ever so violently stretched that it could not possibly be stretched any more, yet the pressure of which is felt long before the final limit is reached, and felt more severely the nearer that limit is approached.
control.work: Principles of Political Economy, 1st ed. (1848), vol. 1, Book I ch. XII
control.locator: Book I, Chapter XII, section 2 (law of diminishing return)

notes: Early text is archive.org djvu OCR of the 1848 first edition (Parker); saved file is the OCR with end-of-line hyphenation joined (de-hyphenation only; page headers and footnote debris remain in the file). I checked the early sentence does not occur in the 7th edition (Gutenberg #30107), consistent with Mill's statement that it was cancelled. The span starts at the Preface and runs to the end of volume 1. Announced passage says the first edition opposed Socialism and that this was cancelled for 'a more advanced opinion' but does not itself state the new view (the 'class us decidedly under ... Socialists' sentence is 70 lines earlier in the same chapter). Claeys's article argues the shift was more of emphasis than a real change of mind, so this case is 'documented' but arguable. No unannounced passage: the later Principles editions are the same work as the early text.

thesis: Whether ethics (the law of equal freedom and rights) rests on God's will/purpose (Social Statics) or on a purely naturalistic evolutionary account (Justice, Principles of Ethics).

early.text: On referring back to Chapter IV., we shall find that the denial of rights amounts to a libel on the Deity. For, as we there saw, that which a man has a right to, is that which God intended for him. And to say that man has no right to freedom of action, is to say that God did not mean him to have it.
early.work: Social Statics (1851), Chapter VI "First Principle", section 4
early.locator: Chapter VI, section 4 (the Deity / "libel on the Deity")

announced.text: This work covers a field which, to a considerable extent, coincides with that covered by Social Statics, published in 1850; though the two differ, alike in extent, in form, and partially in their ideas. One difference is that what there was in my first book of supernaturalistic interpretation has disappeared, and the interpretation has become exclusively naturalistic — that is, evolutionary. With this difference may be joined the concomitant difference, that whereas a biological origin for ethics was, in Social Statics, only indicated, such origin has now been definitely set forth;
announced.work: Justice, Part IV of The Principles of Ethics, Preface

unannounced.text: As, from the evolution point of view, human life must be regarded as a further development of sub-human life, it follows that from this same point of view, human justice must be a further development of sub-huma'n justice. For convenience the two are here separately treated, but they are essentially of the same nature, and form parts of a continuous whole.
unannounced.work: Justice, Part IV of The Principles of Ethics, Chapter III

control.text: Hence the several rights deducible from that law must appertain equally to both sexes. This might have been thought a self-evident truth, needing only to be stated to meet with universal acceptation. There are many, however, who either tacitly, or in so many words, express their dissent from it.
control.work: Social Statics (1851), Chapter XVI "The Rights of Women"
control.locator: Chapter XVI "The Rights of Women", section 1

notes: Both texts are archive.org OCR (Google scan of Social Statics; saved files have end-of-line hyphenation joined, nothing else changed; the 1851 typography puts a space before ; and : in the OCR, so I avoided passages with that). Social Statics is dated 1851 on the title page but was published at the end of 1850. The secondary page is a weak one (tov.com essay): it says Spencer stated any supernaturalistic residue in Social Statics had been eliminated; the real documentation is Spencer's own preface (the announced passage). The Stanford, IEP and Wikipedia Spencer pages I opened do not document this shift. The control passage is about sex equality and avoids the theological premise, but its 'that law' derives from the earlier chapter's Divine-will argument; the equal-rights conclusion itself survives in Justice.

thesis: Whether the fossil record gives evidence of progressive modification of animal forms (and so of evolution) among the higher vertebrates (Huxley's 1862 address says palaeontology negatives progressive modification; his 1870 address softens this and finds a clear balance for evolution in the higher vertebrates).

early.text: In these groups there is abundant evidence of variation--none of what is ordinarily understood as progression; and, if the known geological record is to be regarded as even any considerable fragment of the whole, it is inconceivable that any theory of a necessarily progressive development can stand, for the numerous orders and families cited afford no trace of such a process.
early.work: Geological Contemporaneity and Persistent Types of Life (Address to the Geological Society, 1862)
early.locator: Main body: the invertebrate/vertebrate survey, before the numbered summary of conclusions

announced.text: When I addressed you in 1862, I should have been bold indeed had I suggested that palaeontology would before long show us the possibility of a direct transition from the type of the lizard to that of the ostrich. At the present moment, we have, in the _Ornithoscelida_, the intercalary type, which proves that transition to be something more than a possibility; but it is very doubtful whether any of the genera of _Ornithoscelida_ with which we are at present acquainted are the actual linear types by which the transition from the lizard to the bird was effected.
announced.work: Palaeontology and the Doctrine of Evolution (Presidential Address to the Geological Society, 1870)
announced.locator: Review of the higher-vertebrate evidence ("Ornithoscelida"), after "Thus far I have endeavoured to expand"

control.text: In anatomy, where such correspondence of position has constantly to be spoken of, it is denoted by the word "homology" and its derivatives; and for Geology (which after all is only the anatomy and physiology of the earth) it might be well to invent some single word, such as "homotaxis" (similarity of order), in order to express an essentially similar idea.
control.work: Geological Contemporaneity and Persistent Types of Life (Address to the Geological Society, 1862)
control.locator: Opening discussion of synchronism vs homotaxis

notes: Both addresses are in Gutenberg #10060 (Collected Essays vol. VIII, Macmillan 1894), a single file; the two b_spans are the two address ranges in it (1862: essay IX, 1870: essay XI, Huxley's own text and footnotes). The 1870 address reprints the 1862 conclusions in quotation, so the 1862 sentence also appears there; the early passage was taken from the 1862 address's own text. Announced passage contrasts 1862 and 1870 and states the new view (an intercalary reptile-bird type proves the transition 'more than a possibility'); the more explicit 'softening the somewhat Brutus-like severity with which, in 1862, I dealt with a doctrine' sentence sits in the same section and is the alternative if the strictest 'I was wrong' wording is needed (it states no new view). The Wikipedia Huxley page I opened says he began with a 'persistent types' predilection and later moved away; it does not date the shift to 1862/1870. The Wikisource DNB page (opened) lists the 1870 horse address.

thesis: Whether the self-effacing, compassionate 'saint' and idealism are the goal of nature and the highest human ideal (Schopenhauer as Educator, 1874) or pity and idealism are decadent weaknesses to be overcome (Ecce Homo, 1888).

early.text: Finally, Nature needs the saint. In him the ego has melted away, and the suffering of his life is, practically, no longer felt as individual, but as the spring of the deepest sympathy and intimacy with all living creatures: he sees the wonderful transformation scene that the comedy of "becoming" never reaches, the attainment, at length, of the high state of man after which all nature is striving, that she may be delivered from herself.
early.work: Schopenhauer as Educator (Thoughts out of Season, Part II)

announced.text: It is called a book for free spirits: almost every sentence in it is the expression of a triumph--by means of it I purged myself of everything in me which was foreign to my nature. Idealism is foreign to me: the title of the book means: "Where ye see ideal things I see--human, alas! all-too-human things!" ... I know men better.
announced.locator: "Why I Write Such Excellent Books", Human, All-too-Human, section 1

unannounced.text: What I reproach the pitiful with is, that they are too ready to forget shame, reverence, and the delicacy of feeling which knows how to keep at a distance; they do not remember that this gushing pity stinks of the mob, and that it is next of kin to bad manners--that pitiful hands may be thrust with results fatally destructive into a great destiny, into a lonely and wounded retirement, and into the privileges with which great guilt endows one. The overcoming of pity I reckon among the noble virtues;
unannounced.work: Ecce Homo, "Why I Am So Wise"

control.text: Yes, the university philosophy should have on its monument, "It has hurt nobody." But this is rather the praise one gives to an old woman than to a goddess of truth; and it is not surprising that those who know the goddess only as an old woman are the less men for that, and are naturally neglected by the real men of power.
control.work: Schopenhauer as Educator (Thoughts out of Season, Part II)

notes: Weaker documentation than the others. The announced passage (Ecce Homo on Human, All-too-Human) says outright that Nietzsche purged himself of foreign idealism and that his tone 'has completely changed', but about idealism in general, not Schopenhauer or the saint by name; Nietzsche also claims in Ecce Homo that Schopenhauer as Educator is really 'Nietzsche as Educator', i.e. denies a break. The Philosophy Now page I opened documents the early praise of Schopenhauer and later rejection of pity. The Ecce Homo file is derived from Gutenberg #52190: translator's introduction, translator's footnotes and the poetry removed; I did not otherwise alter the text. Underscores are Gutenberg's italics markup. Section numbers are my best reading of the file's structure and not verified.
